title: Why FFmpeg -c copy cuts the wrong start
fullTitle: FFmpeg -c copy: You Asked for 3 Seconds, You Got 0.52

endCard.line: The full film is on the channel

scenes.narration: You ask FFmpeg for three seconds, starting at seven and a half, with dash c copy. You get thirteen frames. Half a second. Where did the rest go?

Same clip, a keyframe every five seconds. Seek before the input: the clip starts at seven point five two seconds, with seventy five frames. Correct. But the file holds one hundred thirty eight packets, and sixty three are hidden pre-roll.

Move the flag after the input. Now the clip starts at ten seconds, the next keyframe, and holds thirteen frames. A copy can only begin on a keyframe. Re-encode, and it starts on frame one eighty eight, with seventy four frames.

The order of flags matters when you re-encode too. Dash s s five before the input, dash t o ten after it: a ten second clip, source five to fifteen. Both before the input: five seconds. Or use dash t for a length.

So put keyframes where you cut. Dash g one hundred is only a maximum: keyframes land at zero, three point two, and six point eight, on the scene cuts. Add dash s c underscore threshold zero for a strict grid: zero, four, eight.
Or place them yourself, where you will cut. Dash force underscore key underscore frames three point two, six point eight, and they land exactly there.

We tested it on a numbered clip. Three seconds from seven and a half is ninety frames, two twenty five to three fourteen. Seek before the input, dash t for the length, re-encode: exactly those. The control, a copy with the seek after the input: fifteen frames from three hundred.
A plain copy shows the right ninety frames, but carries a hundred sixty five packets. Force keyframes at seven point five and ten point five, and the copy gives ninety frames and ninety packets.

From the end, dash s s e o f minus three should give ninety frames. Re-encoded, it does. With copy and a keyframe every hundred frames, you get a hundred frames, three point three three three seconds. Keyframe every ten: exactly ninety.

The end has the same problem. Dash shortest with copy stops the picture at seventy three of a hundred twenty five frames. Dash t three with copy gives seventy seven. Only a re-encode gives seventy five.

Exact cut: seek before the input, dash t for the length, re-encode. Instant cut: keyframes at the cut, then copy. Always check the frame count with ffprobe. Measured on ffmpeg six point one point one. Not tested: real footage, players, other encoders.
captions: Measured on ffmpeg 6.1.1. Not tested: real footage.
